summary: This informational memo reviews several existing Quality-of-Service signalling protocols for IP networks. The aim is to learn from them, avoid common misconceptions, and avoid mistakes when designing new protocols.

eli5.summary: Before building a new traffic-priority system, this document studies the old ones to see what worked and what did not.

questions: lessons from rsvp and other qos protocols
what is rsvp and how does it work
subtitle: What works and what does not in traffic priority signaling protocols

tldr.problem: RSVP and other QoS signaling protocols aim to request and reserve network resources for traffic flows, but they face challenges in complexity, performance, scalability, security, and mobility that designers of new protocols should learn from.
tldr.mechanism: The document reviews RSVP's design (soft state, two-pass signaling, receiver-initiated reservations), discusses its extensions to MPLS, traffic engineering and DiffServ, analyzes transport and performance issues, then compares alternative protocols like YESSIR, Boomerang, and INSIGNIA.
tldr.outcome: The analysis identifies key design tradeoffs (simplicity vs. functionality, bandwidth vs. setup latency) and lessons learned, informing the design of the Next Steps in Signaling (NSIS) protocols that address the limitations of RSVP.

today: RFC 4094 is Informational and remains a key reference for understanding the strengths and limitations of QoS signaling protocols. RSVP-TE continues to be widely deployed for MPLS traffic engineering. The document's analysis informed the design of NSIS (Next Steps in Signaling), which aims to create a simpler, more general signaling framework that addresses the lessons learned from RSVP. The security and mobility limitations identified here are still relevant considerations for modern network protocol design.

sections.title: The Evolution of QoS Signaling
sections.content:
For decades, the Internet was designed to treat all traffic equally, using a best-effort model. As real-time applications like video and voice became important, networks needed a way for applications to request guaranteed quality of service—ensuring low delay, preventing packet loss, or guaranteeing minimum bandwidth. QoS signaling protocols let applications and network nodes coordinate these resource requests across the network.

RSVP was designed in the early 1990s to provide end-to-end QoS signaling for multicast applications, where one sender transmits to many receivers with different quality needs. Other protocols like ST-II, YESSIR, and Boomerang have been proposed as alternatives. This document learns from them to avoid mistakes in future protocol design.
sections.eli5: Phones and video need to work without delays or dropped calls. Networks need a way to say "please give this traffic priority." Different ways to ask have different strengths and weaknesses.

sections.title: How RSVP Works and Its Extensions
sections.content:
RSVP's core design: A sender announces traffic characteristics in Path messages; receivers respond with Resv messages to reserve resources. Unlike sender-initiated protocols, receiver-initiated reservation scales well with many heterogeneous receivers in multicast. RSVP uses soft state (states timeout if not refreshed) rather than hard state that must be explicitly deleted. Merging reduces signaling when multiple receivers request similar resources.

RSVP has evolved far beyond its original intent. RSVP-TE uses RSVP to establish label-switched paths in MPLS networks, controlling traffic engineering. GMPLS extends RSVP-TE to optical and switching fabrics. RSVP integrates with DiffServ, ATM, IPsec, and 3GPP. These extensions show RSVP's flexibility but also its growing complexity: tens of extensions, new message types, objects for policy, refresh reduction, aggregation, and diagnostic messages.
sections.eli5: RSVP asks receivers to say what quality they need, rather than senders deciding. The same messages set up resources, keep them alive by repeating, and tear them down. It evolved to control telephone calls and optical switching, but each new use adds more complexity.

sections.title: Performance and Transport Problems
sections.content:
RSVP has significant performance and scalability limitations. Message handling is complex: routers must parse variable-length objects, merge reservations, maintain per-flow state. Processing overhead comes not just from the protocol data (objects, message types) but also from user-space daemons that handle RSVP, memory management, and system calls. In one implementation, memory management alone consumed 17 percent of execution cost, and RSVP-routing integration added 11 percent overhead.

Messaging also strains resources. RSVP has no good delivery mechanism: if a message is lost, the next retry is the refresh interval later (default 30 seconds). RFC 2961 introduced staged refresh timers to retransmit until acknowledged, but this added complexity. Message packing (bundling) helps: one implementation improved capacity from 2,000 to over 7,000 sessions per router. The MTU problem is unresolved: RSVP messages cannot span multiple datagrams, limiting security data that can be included. Fortunately, MPLS deployments work around this by using large MTUs or keeping per-session data small.
sections.eli5: RSVP makes routers work hard to track each flow, remembers state that might be lost, and creates large messages that might exceed network link sizes. Small tricks help, but the fundamental design does not scale easily to millions of flows.

sections.title: Security Vulnerabilities and Mobility Challenges
sections.content:
RSVP provides hop-by-hop integrity and authentication via INTEGRITY objects using keyed message digests, but this is insufficient for modern networks. The protocol lacks non-repudiation, protection against message deletion, two-way peer authentication, and proper key management. Security policy data is protected only between policy-aware nodes, not end-to-end. When users or applications authenticate via other means (like SIP), RSVP cannot securely reference those credentials.

Mobility is another weak point. When a mobile node changes location and gets a new IP address, the flow filters no longer identify the flow, invalidating the reservation until a new refresh with updated filters. RSVP cannot autonomously repair reservations when the path changes; it relies on routing protocols to notify RSVP of changes, which Mobile IP does not always do. Standard RSVP refresh intervals (30 seconds) are too long for mobile handovers. Extensions like Localized RSVP and Mobile RSVP attempt fixes using advance reservations at neighboring access points, but they require topological knowledge and explicit handover prediction, limiting applicability.
sections.eli5: RSVP does not verify that the person asking for priority is authorized and then keep that message safe. When you move to a new WiFi network, your quality-of-service request becomes invalid until you ask again, which takes 30 seconds.

sections.title: Alternative QoS Signaling Protocols
sections.content:
Alternative protocols sought to address RSVP's complexity and scalability. YESSIR (one-way, sender-initiated signaling built on RTCP) is simpler and has lower bandwidth consumption than RSVP's two-way model, but requires application support and routers to inspect RTCP packets. Boomerang uses a single message type over ICMP with minimal processing overhead, but provides no multicast support, no security, and lacks functionality compared to RSVP; it is also vulnerable to firewalls that drop ICMP.

INSIGNIA is designed for mobile ad-hoc networks, embedding QoS signaling directly in data packets via IP header options (in-band signaling), avoiding separate control messages. It supports implicit mobility and minimal signaling but assumes routers understand flow labels and lacks any security framework. Inter-domain protocols like BGRP, SICAP, and DARIS aggregate reservations across domain boundaries to reduce state, trading aggregation complexity for scalability in backbone networks.
sections.eli5: Some protocols try to be simpler (YESSIR, Boomerang) but lose features. Others blend signaling into data packets (INSIGNIA) or bundle reservations across many customers (BGRP, DARIS). Each trades off something: security, simplicity, multicast support, or mobile friendliness.

sections.title: Lessons for Future Signaling Protocols
sections.content:
The document concludes that soft-state reservation with flow merging is useful and proven effective. But complexity affects implementation and performance, and security (especially authentication, authorization, and signaling message protection) is underdeveloped in most protocols. RSVP has tools for security (INTEGRITY objects, policy interface) but they are insufficient for dynamic and mobile environments where predistributed keys and manual policies do not work.

Future protocols should learn that there are tradeoffs between functionality and simplicity, bandwidth consumption and setup latency. RSVP's two-way signaling suits multicast and long-lived flows but may be overkill for short-lived request-reply interactions. New applications (firewall control, NAT traversal, active network code injection) have different requirements than traditional QoS. A next-generation signaling protocol should handle reliable messaging, message packing, MTU fragmentation, and low-volume triggered messages—not by reusing RSVP's transport but by building something simpler from the ground up.
sections.eli5: RSVP proved that soft state works well, but future protocols should be simpler, handle security properly, and not assume every flow will last forever or that all applications need multicast support.
